All-New First-Ever BMW iX5 M Electric SUV Loses All Camouflage and Dresses in Java Green – Rendering
6 photos
Photo: kelsonik / Instagram
When it comes to the premium automaker from Bavaria, BMW , opinions are divided about the success or failure of the Neue Klasse design and the decision to mix it with a completely new platform dedicated to EVs. But even if it’s not a hit, it won’t be due to BMW’s lack of trying.
There are several Neue Klasse models that are already out, like the second-generation BMW iX3 and the i3 Sedan; the all-new X5 plus the G50 BMW 3 Series, and more are coming. Many more, actually, as our spy photographer partners have incessantly spied on things like the BMW X2 LCI (Life Cycle Impulse – a facelift), the first-ever BMW i3 Touring, Alpina’s first car from the BMW-owned era – a V8 luxury sedan that hit 186 mph during testing, and more.
The BMW X5, in particular, is an interesting case. The G65, the fifth iteration of the mid-size luxury crossover SUV, started production during the final month of summer with BMW's Neue Klasse style all over it and no less than five powertrain options. Alas, to allow such great expansion of the technical possibilities, BMW made compromises.
So, on the outside and inside, the BMW X5 is Neue Klasse through and through, but under the body the older Cluster Architecture (CLAR) lives on, allowing the use of gasoline, diesel, plug-in hybrid, as well as battery EV and fuel cell setups. There’s also a China-only long-wheelbase variant, dubbed G78, with elements like the 31.3-inch 8K theater screen carried over from the G70 version of the 7 Series, and BMW should soon kick off the preview and teaser campaign for the high-performance M variants.
That’s plural because the rumor mill firmly believes that BMW will feature the same strategy as with the smaller 3 Series – offering both gasoline and fully electric variants for the BMW X5 M and the first-ever BMW iX5 M. The latter has already been spied – so it wasn’t hard for the members of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators to stop dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI to strip off the camouflage.
For example, Nikita Chuicko, the virtual artist better known as " kelsonik " on social media, thinks that now is the right CGI time to work on BMW's latest performance SUV in its EV form, and shows us the upcoming BMW iX5 M (fully electric version) in renderings dressed in a cool hue of Java Green. It also has funky black alloy wheels plus red brake calipers, and the pixel master even presents his ideation renderings in comparison to the current BMW X5 M.
So, what do you think – yay or nay? By the way, keep in mind that the rumor mill believes the electric version of the BMW X5 M will have somewhere around 800 to 900 brake horsepower, so it won’t be a slouch… View this post on Instagram A post shared by CAR DESIGN | RENDERINGS (@kelsonik)

Nissan Celebrates 75 Years of Patrol, Signals Nameplate's Return to the US With Armada Patrol PRO-4X
38 photos
Photo: Nissan
The Japanese automaker Nissan has decided to mark the occasion of Patrol's 75th anniversary in America, too, although the iconic moniker hasn't been seen there since 1969, almost six decades ago.
Of course, the legendary Nissan Patrol has been alive and well in other regions – the Japanese automaker instead chose to use the Armada moniker starting in 2003. Initially, the first-generation Armada was made in Canton, Mississippi, based on the Nissan Titan pickup truck, but since 2016 the Armada moved to a new production location in Kanda, Kyushu, Japan, and started sharing the platform with the global Nissan Patrol.
The luxury version of both is dubbed the Infiniti QX80 (originally QX56), by the way. Now, Nissan has decided to reintroduce the iconic Patrol nameplate to the United States for the first time since 1969, “bringing one of the brand's most enduring and globally recognized badges back to American roads.” As such, for the 2027 model year, Armada's off-road-focused grade has been renamed Patrol PRO-4X instead of simply PRO-4X.
Nissan is taking advantage of Patrol’s 75th anniversary and marking the occasion in the United States, too, with the 2027 Armada Patrol PRO-4X, which enters production in November 2026, “further strengthens that bond, making the connection between Armada and Patrol closer than at any point in the model's history.” The Nissan Patrol first arrived in the US in 1962 through Datsun dealers, and it was initially among the few Nissan-badged vehicles sold in the US market until the early 1980s.
It was no longer offered after 1969 but “remained a popular choice in other markets, particularly the Middle East, where it has become known for its ability to conquer towering dunes.” Nissan explains a quirk: borrowed from the GT‑R, where it was used to keep the power up during tight corners, the Patrol has a special "scavenger" oil pump that enhances lubrication in driving conditions with “high g-forces,” allowing the SUV to climb even the steepest dunes.
Back to the 2027 Armada Patrol PRO-4X, it will become available soon as production of the renamed grade kicks off this month, and it comes with expanded looks and capability: fresh Nismo rock sliders and a Nismo roof rack, plus optional Nismo Axis wheels mated to BF Goodrich all-terrain tires.
"Patrol has defined adventure for 75 years, earning its reputation on some of the toughest terrain in the world. Bringing the Nissan Patrol name back to America through Armada is a natural fit, with both vehicles sharing the same iconic and proven platform," said Tiago Castro, senior vice president, U.S. Marketing & Sales, Nissan and INFINITI. "Armada Patrol PRO‑4X honors that legendary heritage while carrying its capability and confidence into Nissan's future."
The first outing of the 2027 Nissan Armada Patrol PRO-4X will be at the upcoming 2026 LA Auto Show (November 20-29). The grade has an electronic locking rear differential, Adaptive Electronic Air Suspension, eight selectable drive modes, a metal underbody skid plate, and advanced camera systems like Invisible Hood View, among others.
There’s also pricing information: the 2027 Nissan Armada SL 4x2 starts at $64,290 without destination and handling, which is an additional $2,275. The 4x4 version kicks off at $67,290, and the Armada Platinum 4x4 at $75,790. The renamed Armada Patrol PRO-4X is at least $78,990, while the Nismo and Platinum Reserve 4x4 tower above them at $80,690 and $84,590, respectively.

First-Ever Starship Double-Catch Means Rocket Flying Over Populated Texas, Expect Sonic Booms
31 photos
Photo: SpaceX
In early October, SpaceX finally completed the first flight to orbit of its Starship. It was the culmination of years of test flights, not all of them successful, but just a stepping stone to what Elon Musk's company describes as the Holy Grail of rocketry: full reusability by recovering, in working condition, both Super Heavy and Starship stages.
If the stars align, this historic moment in space exploration could happen as soon as next Friday, November 13, when the 15th flight of the rocket and spacecraft, and the second one to orbit, is scheduled to lift off from Pad 2 at Starbase , Texas.
SpaceX says the launch window for the mission, which lasts for 75 minutes, opens at 4:45 p.m. CT. If the launch goes as planned, the Starship will spend some 22 hours up there, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites into orbit. What happens after that, however, could forever rewrite the rules of space launches.
Flight 15 is when SpaceX will try to catch both stages of the Starship using the Mechazilla launch towers. This would mark the first time an entire orbital system of this size is recovered, which also happens to be SpaceX's ultimate goal.
During the most recent Starship missions, the Super Heavy booster returned to its launch site and was caught by the tower's arms, but the Starship itself went for a splashdown in the ocean. About a week before the flight, SpaceX provided us with the details of Flight 15, and, if you ask me, this is shaping up to be a hell of a flight.
Photo: SpaceX You see, a return to the launch site would require the Starship to come back over populated areas, something that has never happened before. It's a pretty tricky approach, as the company needs to make sure nothing goes wrong. And, by the looks of it, all the pieces seem to be in place for the effort to succeed.
We're told the flight profile has been imagined with opportunities to safely end the mission early if necessary, and strict criteria that must be met for the final portion of the mission to be given the all-clear.
First up, for most of the mission the spacecraft will use the same suborbital trajectory used during Flight 14. This allows SpaceX to direct the second stage over the Indian Ocean, should something go wrong.
If everything is in order, however, Starship will light up a single Raptor sea-level engine to start its orbital insertion burn. Once at its destination, the spacecraft will deploy its payload, and it will then coast for most of the mission, around 21 hours. This is needed so that the Starship aligns itself with the Texas Starbase for return.
Photo: SpaceX The bulk of these 21 hours will be spent by ground teams performing all the checks imaginable on the ship's engines, comms systems, flight computers, navigation sensors, and structural integrity, among others.
Should something not feel right during this stage, teams have several options at their disposal to end the flight early, directing the hardware to designated splashdown areas in the Pacific Ocean, including off Hawaii or Chile.
If everything checks out, though, Starship will perform a deorbit burn using a single Raptor engine . This will place it on a trajectory that starts high above the Pacific Ocean, thousands of miles away from the Texas Starbase.
Coming in from the West of the facility, Starship will use its four control flaps to adjust its flight path, which will take it over some populated areas in northern Mexico and southern Texas, but around the major cities of the Rio Grande Valley.
Photo: SpaceX Passing to the north of South Padre Island and out over the Gulf of Mexico, it will then make its final turn toward Starbase, which will put some of the people living in and near Cameron County right in the path of some sonic booms.
When it approaches Starbase, the Starship will perform its final bellyflop that will put it en route to Pad 2. Its three sea-level Raptor engines will then ignite, flipping the second stage into a vertical position for the catch, and the flaps will be stowed. A single engine will remain operational as it comes within reach of the tower's mechanical arms, which will then close to secure the spacecraft.
The importance of this mission is not lost on SpaceX and all the people involved in the project, as this ability to recover both the booster and the spacecraft is what the company bets on to succeed in helping NASA place human boots on the Moon once more, and, in the mid-term future, send the first crew to Mars.
As usual, Starship Flight 15 will be streamed live by SpaceX on its X channel, and we'll be all over it to bring you all the info and the stunning images usually associated with such space missions.

The line between electric bicycles and electric motorcycles has been getting increasingly blurry – though perhaps not because the vehicles themselves are actually that hard to tell apart.
Instead, much of the confusion comes down to terminology. High-powered electric dirt bikes capable of reaching motorcycle-like speeds are increasingly being referred to as “e-bikes,” despite sharing relatively little with the low-speed electric bicycles millions of Americans use for commuting and recreation.
Now the U.S. bicycle industry is asking federal regulators to make that distinction much clearer.
PeopleForBikes , the bicycle industry’s leading trade association, recently testified before the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), calling for stronger federal regulations that specifically distinguish electric bicycles from higher-powered e-motos and electric dirt bikes.

“E-bikes and e-motos are fundamentally different products, and federal safety regulations need to reflect that distinction,” explained PeopleForBikes Policy and General Counsel Matt Moore. “When high-powered electric dirt bikes are marketed as e-bikes, it creates confusion for consumers and puts the credibility of legitimate e-bikes at risk.”
The Lectric XP4 is typical of a street-legal electric bicycle, unlike e-motos that greatly exceed electric bicycle limits
There’s a real nomenclature problem hiding underneath all of this. The term “e-bike” is widely used as shorthand for “electric bicycle,” but it isn’t exclusively used that way. Motorcycles have been called “bikes” for generations, and motorcycle media and riders will sometimes casually refer to electric motorcycles as “e-bikes” too, just in the way a biker refers to his Harley as his “bike”. In fact, it all comes from the same root. We don’t call motorcyclists “motorists”, do we? No… we call them “bikers”.
All of that makes phrases like “legal e-bike” and “legitimate e-bike” that were even used by PeopleForBikes in its arguments somewhat problematic when discussing proposed regulation. The term “e-bike” simply doesn’t mean anything specific, at least not legally.
What actually matters from a legal standpoint is whether a vehicle meets the codified definition of an electric bicycle, not whether someone calls it an e-bike – especially when the term e-bike is practically applied so broadly. In other words, perhaps part of separating electric bicycles from e-motos is being more precise with the terminology ourselves: “electric bicycle” has a specific regulatory meaning, while “e-bike” has increasingly become a much fuzzier colloquial term. As much as some would want the term “e-bike” to mean something with pedals, it simply doesn’t – at least not in North America.
I’m certainly guilty of this myself in my writing and videos, falling back on the commonly used phrasing instead of the technical legal terminology, but keeping them separated could help with the growing misunderstanding in the industry.
Legal electric bicycles are a far cry from e-motos, but the terminology can often get mixed up
That distinction has become increasingly important as lightweight electric motorcycles and dirt bikes have exploded in popularity . Many feature bicycle-like frames and components, and some even include pedals , but their performance can extend far beyond what federal law defines as a low-speed electric bicycle.
The concern goes beyond mere semantics. When a 50-60 mph (80-100 km/h) electric dirt bike gets lumped into the same category as a 20-28 mph (32-45 km/h) commuter e-bike, crashes and reckless riding involving the former can quickly become part of the public conversation surrounding the latter. That can ultimately influence how lawmakers, regulators, police departments, and the general public view e-bikes as a whole.
In fact, many of the supposed electric bicycle crash figures we’ve seen touted in the news aren’t from electric bicycles at all, but rather from e-moto accidents that have been lumped in with electric bicycles, making the latter appear more dangerous than they truly are.
If street-legal electric bicycles were separated from e-motos in crash statistics, the category would be revealed to be much safer than conventional reporting would have us believe.
E-motos like this Annioki A9 can sometimes look similar to electric bicycles, despite hiding much higher performance
All of this and more has led to PeopleForBikes pushing federal regulators to draw a clearer line.
As part of its CPSC testimony, the organization recommended retaining the existing federal definition of a low-speed electric bicycle while creating a separate definition for e-motos, including machines capable of speeds up to 60 mph (96 km/h). It also called for mandatory electrical safety standards for off-road e-motos, which it says currently fall into a regulatory gap, as well as greater scrutiny of conversion kits capable of turning conventional bicycles into vehicles operating beyond their original structural design limits.
The testimony came as the CPSC considers new mandatory federal battery safety standards for e-bikes and other electric mobility devices . PeopleForBikes says it supports stronger battery standards, while recommending that regulators rely on existing UL standards without modification.
PeopleForBikes is also asking the CPSC and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to coordinate enforcement against e-motos that evade federal requirements.
None of this means e-motos are inherently bad. They’re incredibly fun machines, and there’s a rapidly growing market for them. But a 60 mph (96 km/h) electric dirt bike isn’t an electric bicycle simply because it looks vaguely like one.
And increasingly, the bicycle industry wants regulators to make sure everyone understands the difference.
E-motos like the Juiced Nomadix can be great fun, but are meant to be used off of public streets. Keep it in the dirt!

By: Colin McClelland November 9, 2026
A takeover that brought Coeur Mining (TSX, NYSE: CDE) into Canada, a strategy connecting uranium production with reactor technology and four decades spent building a gold giant underpin The Northern Miner ’s latest leadership awards.
Coeur CEO Mitchell Krebs is Mining Person of the Year, Cameco (TSX: CCO; NYSE: CCJ) president and chief operating officer Grant Isaac receives Operator of the Year, and Agnico Eagle Mines (TSX, NYSE: AEM) chair Sean Boyd earns the Lifetime Achievement Award.
“It wasn’t really about, and hasn’t really been about, how big we are, how many mines we’ve built,” Boyd told The Northern Miner . “It’s more about how we did it, and just trying to do things the right way.”
The three honourees pursued different paths to growth. Each invested through industry cycles, strengthened existing operations and built teams that could sustain the business beyond any one transaction.
Krebs adds Canada
Boyd and Isaac are due to receive their awards on stage Nov. 29 at The Northern Miner ’s London Symposium . Krebs is set to receive his award at The Northern Miner ’s Rome Symposium , which runs May 26–27, 2027.
Coeur CEO Mitchell Krebs is The Northern Miner’s Mining Person of the Year.
For Krebs, the defining move was Coeur’s acquisition of New Gold, completed in March. The takeover added Rainy River in Ontario and New Afton in British Columbia, giving the Chicago-based producer its first operating Canadian mines and a substantial copper business.
The deal capped a rebuilding effort that began after Krebs became CEO in 2011. Moving the company out of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, brought fresh ideas into a business with roots there dating back to the late 1920s, Krebs told The Northern Miner in an Oct. 16 interview. Coeur sold assets outside North America and reinvested in mines it decided to keep, including Rochester in Nevada.
The Rochester expansion strained Coeur’s finances, but as the enlarged silver-gold mine began to deliver, it gave the company the momentum to buy SilverCrest Metals, Krebs said. That acquisition, completed in February 2025, brought cash and the high-grade, lower-cost Las Chispas mine in Mexico. It helped Coeur repay debt and repair its balance sheet before buying New Gold.
Coeur recorded negative free cash flow of $297 million (C$416 million) in 2023. Krebs said in October he expected it to generate close to $1.5 billion in 2026, even with only nine months of contributions from the New Gold mines.
“Before we were consumers of capital, now we’re generators of a significant amount of cash flow, and our focus now is really turning to capital allocation with a much longer-term perspective,” Krebs said.
The immediate priority is integrating the acquisitions and finding more mineralization around existing mines. Coeur plans to spend about $158 million on exploration this year, almost 50% more than last year, Krebs said.
“I mean, it’s an extractive business, right?” he said. “So if you’re not finding more ounces, you need to be adding new ounces through external opportunities.”
Isaac builds demand
Cameco’s 49% interest in Westinghouse Electric connects its uranium operations with reactor technology, fuel fabrication and servicing. Helping utilities build reactors could create decades of demand for Cameco’s uranium and fuel services, Isaac told The Northern Miner in an October interview about the company’s growth strategy.
Cameco president and chief operating officer Grant Isaac receives The Northern Miner’s Operator of the Year award.
“Over the long run, the value of selling uranium for 80 to 100 years is way greater than the five to seven years of building a reactor,” Isaac said. “So think of it as our strategy is about not waiting for others to create new demand for us. We’re out there building our own demand.”
At its mines, Cameco bases production decisions on long-term contracts with utilities, Isaac said. At McArthur River in Saskatchewan, unexpected clay slowed the ground-freezing work needed to reach new mining areas. Management held off on spending heavily to recover lost time because customer commitments didn’t justify the cost, he said.
About 30% of Cameco’s licensed and built production capacity was either being held back or on care and maintenance, Isaac said. That gives the company room to increase output as utilities sign contracts.
Boyd’s lasting culture
Boyd’s recognition reflects Agnico’s transformation from a regional producer with one mine into Canada’s largest mining company. During his 24 years as CEO, its market value increased more than 100-fold.
His account begins with founder Paul Penna’s generosity and the relationships that persuaded a young auditor to join the company in 1985. As Boyd recalled in his Lifetime Achievement profile , that became Agnico’s “culture of the heart,” placing employees and communities alongside shareholder returns.
When safety concerns forced the closure of the Goldex mine in 2011, Agnico committed to paying employees for three months. During the 2013 gold price collapse, it took a measured approach to spending and jobs, preserving the strength to pursue subsequent opportunities.
Those included Canadian Malartic, while the 2022 Kirkland Lake Gold merger added Detour Lake, Macassa and Fosterville.
Asked what Penna would recognize today, Boyd returned to the company’s character.
“He’d recognize the feel,” Boyd said. “He’d be prouder of the fact that we did it in a way where it still feels the same.” Print

“Sure, diesel is high, but electric trucks don’t work.” It’s a common refrain these days – especially from people selling diesel trucks. Perception lags reality, however, and the reality is that these electric semi trucks are covering more than 600 miles per day, seven days a week.
Over the course of the last year, Hendrik Müller , managing partner of DEFRU Logistik GmbH has transformed his company’s shipping fleet, switching thirty of their HD prime movers (semi trucks) to electric power and immediately putting the Mercedes-Benz eActros 600s to work, covering 1,000 km (~620 miles) of German highways each and every day.
Benjamin Budick, a Senior Manager, Own Retail Mercedes-Benz Trucks Dortmund & Haan, took to LinkedIn to announce the successful deployment, and posted some great pictures of the handover showing the big Mercedes trucks in full DEFRU livery.
Mercedes’ eActros 600 packs a whopping, 621 kWh battery that helps the trucks cover 500 km per charge, allowing fleets to move goods between ports and regional fulfillment centers, charging along the way , or while they’re getting loaded and unloaded at their destination, all the while saving the fleet serious money – even before the latest Iran War sent diesel prices skyrocketing .

That big battery sends electrons to Mercedes-Benz’s proprietary electric drive axles, which deliver 1.61 kWh / mile efficiency while rolling out at an average of 36 metric tons (~79,400 lbs.) combined vehicle weight – specs that rivals the theoretical efficiency claims of the Tesla Semi . Except in the real world. And in winter .
The company recently expanded its eActros lineup to include over 40 possible configurations, giving customers a choice of two cab designs, two or three battery packs, multiple wheelbases and new axle configurations, covering everything from short-haul drayage to serious, off highway vocational work.

By Angelo Mathais India correspondent
9 November 2026
A new storm of stakeholder disputes, and potential operational disruption, is brewing across Indian ports over policy changes by container lines on empty-container handling and associated depot charges.
The loading and unloading of empty boxes at yards is the flashpoint for discontent and disagreement between supply chain intermediaries and carriers.
Maersk, for example, has substantially raised its lift-on/lift-off (lo-lo) charges for empties moving via Mundra, India’s busiest container port and the primary gateway for the hinterlands around Delhi.
The revision, implemented from 1 November, effectively more than doubled the rates shippers had been charged, from $23 to $51 per 20ft empty box, and from $31 to $67 per 40ft, plus local taxes.
“Customers are requested to take notice of this change and make the necessary arrangements to ensure smooth container pick-up and drop-off operations,” Maersk told customers.
Additionally, the carrier advised them to settle the charges directly with nominated depot service providers, an issue that had already become contentious at Chennai port.
Now the controversy is becoming industry-wide, as sources expect other carriers to issue similar trade notices for their ’empty’ operations at Mundra. Ondeed, one liner source told The Loadstar : “We are discussing the matter.”
At Chennai, MSC seems to be facing the brunt of a trade pushback against the practice of routing empty tariff collections through third-party depot vendors, which cargo agents claim opens the market to an unregulated environment.
“MSC has taken the lead in implementing this collection practice in Chennai, following which other shipping lines have initiated similar measures,” the Chennai Customs Brokers Association (CCBA) noted.
The CCBA claimed the policy shift was fraught with “serious economic and operational implications for cargo agents”, as it had seen third-party vendors keep inflating tariffs once taken over.
“Allowing third-party vendors to collect additional charges without adequate transparency or accountability would create an open-ended financial burden on the export/import trade, particularly customs brokers,” it said.
The association also claimed its member agents – an integral part of India’s supply chains – were being increasingly ‘caught in the middle’, with exporters and importers refusing to reimburse the add-ons that had found their way onto final customer bills.
Indeed, the CCBA has threatened to boycott MSC shipments if the new practice is not reversed by 15 November, and told The Loadstar : “Our association will follow the same stance in the case of other shipping lines seeking similar depot arrangements.”
According to sources, some carriers serving JNPA (Nhava Sheva) have also switched to the practice of permitting nominated yards to collect lo-lo charges directly from shippers, despite strong resistance from the cargo-handling community.
“Any logistics cost increase ultimately goes straight down to the shipper, making it difficult to explain, or sort out,” one forwarder said.
“Intermediaries add price mark-ups, an area Indian logistics policymakers have been trying to streamline through reforms,” added one industry observer.

Tesla Cybertruck production April 2024
Elon Musk now claims Cybertruck orders “far exceed” Tesla’s production rate, and that the truck isn’t being killed because it’s unprofitable. It’s his second explanation in three days for ending the pickup.
The problem is that Tesla’s own numbers say the opposite. The Cybertruck line has been running at roughly a quarter of its installed capacity, and Tesla spent all of 2026 discounting, re-trimming, and repricing the truck to find buyers.
Here’s what Musk posted on X overnight:
“The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people. This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media, but rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.”
The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people. This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported… https://t.co/rGmNKV3ILs — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 9, 2026
He was quote-tweeting a Tesla fan telling people to “get it while you can.” So yes, this is also a sales pitch.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
On Friday, Musk announced Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around mid-2027 “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” That was the first story. Now it’s about “complexity” and “opportunity cost.” Let’s go through it.
“Order rate far exceeds our production rate”
Tesla controls its production rate. That’s the flaw in this claim.
Tesla built the Cybertruck supply chain for 250,000 units a year, and its latest shareholder letter still lists more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. In Q3 2026, it delivered 8,295 “Other Models.” With Model S and Model X out of production, we estimated 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks . That’s a 30,000-a-year pace, down 48% year-over-year in that category.
If orders had been outrunning production at any point this year, Tesla had about 95,000 units of idle annual capacity sitting right there. It didn’t use it.
And companies with a backlog don’t behave like Tesla did. In February, it offered a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.” It pulled a single-motor RWD version after just 173 sales. It leaned on Musk’s own companies too: SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025 , about 19% of US registrations that quarter once you add his other firms.
Cox Automotive estimates US Cybertruck sales fell from 14,416 in Q3 2024 to 3,519 in Q1 2026 and 3,744 in Q2. It’s a demand problem everyone could see.
So if orders spiked this weekend, there’s an obvious reason: Musk told the world on Friday that the truck is going away. A last-call rush on a discontinued vehicle is not proof that it was selling.
“Will have to return deposits for a lot of people”
Tesla has been sitting on Cybertruck deposits it was never going to fill for years.
Musk touted more than a million reservations, and crowdsourced tallies put the list near 2 million by 2023 . Its best US quarter, by Cox Automotive’s estimate, was 14,416 trucks. The reservation book was a vanity number, not an order book.
Two weeks ago, Tesla cancelled the Cybertruck for Australia and New Zealand and refunded deposits people had paid in 2019. Returning deposits is something Tesla was already doing because it couldn’t sell the truck in those markets, not because it was swamped.
“Not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable”
This one is a straw man. Our reporting, and most of the coverage Friday, was about sales, not margins. The truck sells at about 12% of the volume Tesla planned for.
Tesla doesn’t disclose Cybertruck margins, so Musk can say whatever he wants here and nobody can check it. But he’s the one who said in 2023 that Tesla had “dug our own grave with Cybertruck” because of how hard it was to build profitably.
And look at what Tesla did the same day it announced the end of production: it raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the cheapest trim. The cheapest orderable Cybertruck went from $69,990 in early August to $92,490. You do that to squeeze margin out of the last trucks, not because the line was printing money.
The “opportunity cost” argument proves our point
Follow Musk’s logic to the end. If the Cybertruck were profitable and orders really outran production, killing it would mean walking away from guaranteed profit for a robotaxi that had 463 units registered in Texas as of late October and no proven business yet.
The only way that trade makes sense is if the Cybertruck’s profit at 30,000 units a year is small. Which is another way of saying it doesn’t sell enough.
Giga Texas also has more than 10 million square feet of floor space, and the Cybercab runs on its own “unboxed” line. Tesla can’t make use of the Cybertruck line and floor space was never the constraint. To further adapt his logic for shutting down Cybertruck production, Musk shifted his argument from “space” to Cybercab’s line needing some “smart people”, who he implied work on the Cybertruck.
Musk wrote on Saturday that “there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people” , but Michael So, who led Cybercab new product introduction and was Giga Texas employee #1, left in April for nuclear startup Aalo Atomics. Last month, Tesla lost its Cybercab general assembly lead to Rivian’s R2 program just weeks after the launch. If talent is the bottleneck, it’s the Cybercab team that’s bleeding it.
Electrek’s Take
Musk doesn’t want the Cybertruck to go down in history as a flop, and we get it. It’s his truck. He approved the controversial design, hyped it for four years before it shipped, and boasted that 1 million reservations could translate to 500,000 units a year.
But you can’t run a line at a quarter of capacity, run “10 days only” discounts, pull trims after 173 sales, and sell trucks to your own rocket company, then turn around and tell people demand was never the issue. The data is public. Tesla’s own delivery reports are public.
Our read on what happened is simple. Demand collapsed in 2025 and never came back. Tesla tried every pricing trick it had. When nothing worked, it found a future-facing reason to end it, and now it’s spinning the inevitable end-of-life rush as proof the truck was a hit all along.
Musk loves a big TAM. SpaceX’s IPO filing put its total addressable market at $28.5 trillion , and last month he went further, writing that he sees “a path to SpaceX being worth orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy.”
So apply the same lens to Tesla. Pickups are one of the biggest and most profitable vehicle markets on the planet. Ford sold 801,525 F-Series trucks in the US last year, GM sold 925,656 Silverados and Sierras combined, and Ram moved 374,059. That’s more than 2.1 million trucks from three automakers, easily north of $100 billion a year at today’s transaction prices.

By Charlotte Goldstone
9 November 2026
US companies buying goods on Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) terms have been urged to examine who is responsible for their customs declarations, after US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) introduced new requirements for foreign importers of record (IORs).
The interim final rule, published in the Federal Register last week takes effect on 5 January, with new conditions for foreign IORs making both formal and informal entries into the US, as well as additional verification responsibilities for licensed customs brokers.
Under the rule, a foreign IOR validated under the Customs-Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) programme can make entries itself, or appoint a licensed customs broker that does not have to be CTPAT-validated.
A foreign IOR without CTPAT must designate a broker that is both licensed and CTPAT-validated to make the entry or act as IOR.
Where the foreign party is not the owner or purchaser of the goods, the designated broker must act as the importer of record.
However, the rule also establishes stricter criteria for determining whether a business qualifies as a US IOR.
An individual must be a US citizen or lawful permanent resident, while a company must be organised under US law, located in the country, and at least 51% of its beneficial owners must be US citizens or permanent residents who control the business, or who directly own a significant amount of unencumbered US real estate.
Licensed customs brokers will have to verify a client’s eligibility before declaring it to be a US IOR. They must request and review supporting records, which could include corporate documents, financial statements, and proof of citizenship or permanent residence. Verification records must then be retained for five years.
The development follows CargoTrans’s recent tariff webinar, which examined the risks associated with DDP arrangements , noted that in theory an overseas supplier typically arranging import clearance and paying duties and taxes, offered the US buyer a seemingly simpler route to receiving goods.
But CargoTrans co-CEO Nunzio De Filippis said the new rule made that convenience harder to achieve, adding: “So that easy button that we spoke about just got harder to press.”
He advised buyers to establish exactly who is responsible for the import process when their overseas supplier sells on DDP terms.
“You have to ask them who is the importer record, who is the customs broker, what does that arrangement look like, and does it meet the new requirements?” he said.
“Welcome to the age of strengthening customs enforcement,” he added.
CBP explained the measures were intended to improve visibility of foreign importers, strengthen accountability, and help ensure duties are collected. The agency highlighted difficulties pursuing unpaid duties and enforcing customs requirements against foreign entities with few US assets.
Brokers may request delayed compliance with the new verification requirements before 5 January, but all must be fully compliant by 6 May next year. Comments on the interim final rule are due by 5 January.
For US buyers, the update means a DDP quotation alone is no guarantee that the underlying import arrangements meet the new requirements. Buyers should establish who is named as the IOR, which broker is filing the entry, and whether the relevant parties satisfy CBPconditions.

One in six leaders say an AI tool mishandled supplier or customer data at their company in the past year, according to new research from InstaLILY. That figure rose to 22% among supply chain respondents.
What’s Related
Most respondents (81%) reported no incident, while 3% were unsure. The research did not establish how serious the incidents were or whether data left the business.
The findings come from a Pollfish survey launched Oct. 9 of 250 managers and executives in supply chain, logistics, distribution, and wholesale whose companies use AI in daily work.
Does AI have too much info?
The findings show how far AI has reached into commercial data. Seventy-eight percent of respondents said their AI tools can access customer pricing and margins, and the same share said AI can reach customer purchase histories. Sixty-seven percent said their tools can access supplier pricing and rebate data.
Confidence is high anyway. Eighty-seven percent said they are very or somewhat confident their AI tools keep supplier and customer data separated, even though only 32% said that data sits in separate systems.
RELATED STORIES: 1 in 4 IT Leaders Say AI Mistakes Have Hurt Their Business | Procurement Leaders See AI Skills as Essential, but Few Feel Ready
Customers and suppliers are paying attention. 63% said their company has been asked how it protects supplier or customer data. Of those, 47% said the question affected a decision about a vendor, software or AI tool.
The top barrier to keeping data separate was tools not built with that in mind (22%), followed closely by cost (21%) and a lack of technical expertise (20%). 90% said they would be more likely to choose AI built for distribution and supply chain over a general-purpose tool if it offered better control over that data. InstaLILY sells AI agents for distributors and logistics companies.
About half said their employer would bear the most responsibility for an exposure, compared with 23% who pointed to the AI vendor.
Questions to Ask Before Expanding AI
The report lays out several steps for companies widening their use of AI:
Map what each tool can reach. That includes AI features built into existing software, not just standalone tools.
Test the permissions. Can an employee pull up account terms they shouldn’t see? Could a customer quote reveal a confidential supplier rebate?
Make vendors prove it. Ask providers to run a realistic workflow with test data and tell you what records they can access when investigating an incident.
Have an answer ready. Prepare clear explanations for suppliers and customers who ask how you handle their information.
Review access before consolidating. Seventy-eight percent rate cutting down to fewer AI vendors as a high or moderate priority for the next year. The report advises reassessing who needs access before moving workflows to a new platform.

ZURICH — Swiss voters will decide on Nov. 29 whether to block a bill relaxing curbs on weapons exports, in a referendum that raises questions about Switzerland’s evolving neutral tradition and is strongly opposed by the arms industry.
Switzerland follows the 1907 Hague Conventions on neutrality, which prevent it participating in armed conflicts unless directly threatened, or providing military support to any of the parties.
Yet a stance that largely held throughout the Cold War has begun to change since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 prompted Switzerland to deepen its defense ties with European partners and the transatlantic NATO alliance.
Polls suggest the referendum, proposed by a coalition of left-wing parties including Social Democrats, the Greens and others, could go either way.
Some right-wingers have also split from the Swiss People’s Party (SVP) to oppose the amendment, which cannot come into force until the referendum is held.
“In future, Swiss war material could in certain cases be passed to belligerent states,” said Fabian Molina, a lawmaker for the leftist Social Democrats. “That would violate neutrality.”
The amendment is intended to allow arms shipments to 36 Western countries, even if they are involved in active armed conflicts, albeit not for use in those conflicts. Ukraine is not included, however.
It also scraps a requirement for countries to sign a non-re-export declaration upon purchase.
Bern had blocked several countries from sending previously purchased Swiss-made ammunition and combat vehicles to Ukraine, and Germany subsequently excluded Swiss firms from procurement deals, while Denmark and the Netherlands halted orders.
The amendment would, however, not apply to weaponry bought on the previous terms, or bought with the intention of immediately sending it to a third party – thus still excluding Ukraine.
Center Party lawmaker Reto Nause said the law needed to be overhauled to reflect a more dangerous international environment.
“We’re facing a level of threat we haven’t seen since the Second World War,” he said. “Part of being able to defend yourself is having a domestic arms industry, having some production capacity and above all know-how in key technologies.”
The non-re-export declaration would deter NATO countries from buying Swiss armaments because they wanted to be able to share weapons if the alliance was attacked, Nause said.
The affected manufacturers include Germany’s Rheinmetall, which builds anti-drone defense systems in Switzerland, French defense group Thales, small-arms maker SIG Sauer, and more than 100 other companies.
Weapons made in Switzerland
Switzerland was the world’s 17th-largest arms exporter over the past 10 years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
The sector employs 14,000 people and last year, its exports were worth around $1.15 billion.
Manufacturers fear for the future if the law is not amended, arguing that the domestic market is too small, and their supporters say there are another 154,000 jobs in companies making “dual use” products – for military or civilian purposes.
“This is decisive, it’s really ‘go’ or ‘no go’ for the future of the Swiss arms industry,” said Matthias Zoller, general secretary of the Swiss Aeronautics, Security and Defence Association, which represents the industry.
He said it was crucial for Switzerland to have its own armaments industry but, if exports were excessively restricted, manufacturers could simply move abroad.
And if Switzerland could no longer sell arms abroad, it could expect to go to the back of the line for buying new systems or even components from other countries, he said.
Green Party lawmaker Gerhard Andrey said ceding control of where Swiss arms go was “not a neutral choice,” and noted that exports were just below record level last year, despite the restrictions.
Mirjam Hostetmann, leader of the youth wing of the Social Democrats, said relaxing the law could lead to Swiss weapons increasingly being used in civil wars or by rogue governments.
“It’s an illusion to believe that more weapons will guarantee more peace,” she said. “Nobody benefits from these changes apart from the arms industry.”

New Gas Turbine Will Keep AI Cool Before It Gets to Power Supersonic Passenger Plane
19 photos
Photo: Boom Supersonic
I usually take breakthrough news of startups developing revolutionary aircraft with a grain of salt. Not because these guys are not serious about their projects, but because, most of the time, seriousness is not enough to get these projects off the ground, and many of the companies imagining them go bust. But not the guys over at Boom Supersonic, it seems.
The company first caught my eye some six years ago, when I learned of the supersonic airplane it was working on, the Overture . Capable of carrying 80 people at a time, it should fly at speeds of Mach 1.3 (997 mph/1,605 kph), which is enough to get them from one American coast to the other in one and a half hours.
The design is still in the works, and the last time I heard anything about it was when a jet-powered test bed called XB-1 began testing (the program has ended in the meantime), but chances are the production version is still a long time away.
Unlike many other aviation startups, especially the ones struggling to stay afloat, Boom diversified its business at the end of last year, when it announced it will make a natural gas turbine with a capacity of 42 megawatts for the needs of AI data centers.
The turbine, whose breed is called Superpower, was first imagined as a component part of the Symphony engine that's supposed to power the Overture sometime in the future. And at the end of last month, it just got real.
Boom said in late October that the first supersonic turbine core has been completed and is already on location at the company's test site at Colorado Air and Space Port in Watkins, Colorado. And it even has a name.
Going by Sprint Core, the prototype, which bundles together the compressor, combustor, and the high-pressure turbine itself, is not unlike the tech that'll go into the Superpower power generation solution and the Symphony supersonic engine.
Boom will use this piece of hardware and the thousands of sensors that were strapped to it to calibrate the engineering tools at the Superfactory facility in Centennial, South Denver area, and optimize the production of the Superpower design.
By the looks of it, Boom has a better chance of succeeding in making the Overture supersonic plane compared to some of its competitors. The company says part of the money made with selling the Superpower solution (there is talk of an $1.25 billion backlog of orders for the tech) to artificial intelligence infrastructure providers will go into developing the aircraft.
Boom said a while back the Overture had drawn the eye of operators the likes of United Airlines, American Airlines, and Japan Airlines, which have placed around 130 orders for the supersonic plane.
If and when the production of the airplane begins, Boom expects to roll out up to 66 planes per year at another Superfactory in Greensboro, North Carolina.

Mercedes-AMG Wins 2026 Formula 1 Constructors Title Bringing Their Total to Nine
8 photos
Photo: Mercedes-AMG F1 Team/Getty Images
It was an eventful 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix, featuring a mix of inters and softs, shifting weather and various degrees of dryness on the track. In the end, it was Lando Norris who handed McLaren its third victory of the season, while Mercedes-AMG won their ninth constructors' title as George Russell and Kimi Antonelli finished P4 and P5 respectively.
In a vacuum, this would have been a race to forget for the German outfit. After looking like the team to beat in practice, both Mercedes drivers suffered spins during the race - Russell finding himself pointing the wrong way at pit exit, while Antonelli spun just as he was trying to hold onto a lead.
To make matters worse, Antonelli was handed a 5 second penalty after the race for an unsafe pit stop release. The newly crowned World Champion was released straight into the path of Franco Colapinto. Luckily, they managed to avoid each other. However, because Antonelli was already more than 20 seconds ahead of Piastri, the penalty proved technically irrelevant.
Nonetheless, the Silver Arrows did enough to secure the points needed to seal the constructors' title, their first since that spectacular 2021 season that saw Max Verstappen snatch Lewis Hamilton's heart out in Abu Dhabi.
"Winning the world championship is a proud moment for every member of our team. F1 is a people business. The trophies may be handed over at the track, but success starts in our factories, in our meeting rooms, on the simulator, in the machine shops, and with every individual who contributes to our performance," said team principal & CEO, Toto Wolff.
"We will enjoy this achievement because everyone has earned that right. Then, very quickly, our focus will turn to the next challenge. That is the mentality that has shaped this team and will continue to drive us forward. That is more important than ever as today wasn’t an easy afternoon for us. We had the pace to win today but suffered during both transition points."
"We would obviously have liked to finish the job in a more convincing way, but ultimately, we scored the points we needed. These last few races have been challenging at times and today was another difficult one, so there is plenty for us to understand and improve"
Photo: Mercedes-AMG F1 Team/Getty Images Every single member of the team that was interviewed following the race was equally happy for the outcome, although it would have been hard to ignore how one of the drivers looked a little less excited than the other. I'm talking, of course, about George Russell , who wasn't smiling quite as gleefully as his teammate.
Then again, one can hardly hold that against him, since Mercedes could have done much better in terms of helping him fight for the title this year. His 2026 campaign was scarred by a combination of persistent car unreliability and incredibly bad luck. And yes, Antonelli's race execution was superior when it mattered, but still. You can't help but feel bad for the British driver, who's already proven to be one of the most talented names on the grid.

Dying NASA Telescope Leaves Behind 600 HD Movies-Worth of Data, To Be Studied for Years
9 photos
Photo: NASA
Following a last-minute attempt by NASA to save it, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory space telescope has officially ended its mission, and it's now heading for a fiery demise in our planet's atmosphere. It leaves behind, though, a treasure chest of findings that'll keep scientists busy for decades to come.
The Swift telescope, born as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer , departed our world at the end of 2004 with the stated goal of finding and studying the universe's most powerful explosions, gamma-ray bursts, and, additionally, other cosmic objects and events.
The estimated lifetime of the tool back then was just two years, but it was operational for more than ten times as long. And it would have continued to do so for many more years to come, if it weren't for an orbital decay process that slowly but surely ate at its orbit, situated at some 375 miles (604 km) at its furthest.
The Swift started slowly sinking from its orbit a while back, and, for a short period of time, there was hope it could be saved. NASA and its partner Katalyst Space Technologies sent a rescue ship into space, but the mission failed, prompting NASA to officially call it quits.
The observatory made its final observation on October 20, and then sank to an altitude of 171 miles (275 km) above the surface of our planet. From there, it is impossible for it to perform more observations, and it is now closer and closer to reentering the atmosphere and meeting its end over the next few weeks.
As it gets ready to completely bury the project, NASA shared some of the numbers behind the Swift mission. And let me tell you, they are pretty impressive.
During its more than two-decade mission, the telescope looked at over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, including, for the first time, a glimpse of bursts that are generated by merging neutron stars forming black holes, and witnessed more than 1,400 supernova explosions.
It kept track of a number of cosmic objects, including the 3I/ATLAS interstellar comet that crossed our solar system at the end of last year, was witness to stars being eating by black holes, and even conducted an all-sky X-ray survey.
NASA said the Swift observatory generated 1.5 million images with its main instrument, the Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope, amounting, together with all the other data, to an impressive 12 terabytes of information. For the record, that's the size of some 600 high-definition movies put together.
The huge trove of discoveries is likely to form the basis of further discoveries, on top of the already published 7,000 scientific papers.
We will keep an eye on the telescope and report back once it disappears completely from the sky.

Photo: Thai Cargo
By Alex Lennane
9 November 2026
A backlog at Thai Airways’ cargo warehouse at Bangkok Suvarnabhumi is disrupting imports and exports, prompting airlines to restrict Bangkok-bound freight.
Airline accounts on Thursday reported more than 1,000 outstanding cargo lots and 700–800 pallets awaiting breakdown. Neither Thai Airways (TG) nor Airports of Thailand (AOT) has confirmed the current backlog or any recovery date.
AOT said today it had allocated Warehouse 4 in the airport’s free zone for oversized cargo, and was discussing additional space for international imports with Thai Airways and Customs. It was also working to improve shipment tracking, it added.
Thai Airways acknowledged on Friday that rising inbound volumes had left large numbers of unit load devices (ULDs) awaiting breakdown and storage, delaying deliveries, and said it was adding staff and forklifts, seeking more space, and introducing a system to record cargo locations.
Missing or inaccurate storage records have compounded the problem, according to the Thai Airfreight Forwarders Association, leaving agents unable to establish when shipments can be collected. Unprocessed cargo also ties up ULDs needed for subsequent flights.
Thai Airways said it was prioritising shipments that arrived before 23 October while continuing to handle new arrivals.
The Thai Chamber of Commerce warned that delays were raising costs and disrupting production and delivery schedules for manufacturers reliant on imported materials and components. Congested working areas and delayed ULD breakdown were now affecting exports too.
Cathay Cargo has restricted Bangkok-bound freight at least until 15 November to intact ULDs that can be released without breakdown at destination, with exemptions for specified temperature-controlled and special cargo.
The chamber said Singapore Airlines Cargo had also notified customers last week of temporary restrictions on certain shipments, citing disruption to ULD circulation and outbound handling.
UK forwarder Beckchoice separately reported that a 3 November advisory from Thai Airways’ Korea cargo office noted limited acceptance of some transit and Thailand-bound freight between 4–8 November to through or unitised ULDs.
Warnings predate the latest restrictions. Teleport, Expeditors, and Geodis have all flagged congestion at the TG warehouse over the past two months, affecting inbound and outbound handling.
In its latest regional air market update, Expeditors said TG had asked airlines to reduce inbound volumes and had restricted additional charters until further notice. An earlier briefing reported a request to cut inbound cargo by 50% through 7 November.
Expeditors also reported longer queues for weighing and export handover at TG, as import breakdown delays prolonged export processing. At BFS, truck waiting times remained around 24 hours, despite some improvement following warehouse expansion.
Time-sensitive manufacturing inputs are among the goods exposed. WICE Logistics executive Chudech Kongsunthorn told Thai publication The Standard that data centre and electronics investment was driving equipment imports, alongside shipments of semiconductor and electronic parts, medical equipment, and pharmaceuticals. Cargo normally released within 24 hours was taking days or, in some cases, weeks, he said.
Export delays also threaten electronics and other airfreight staples, including fresh food, flowers, gems, and medical goods.
The congestion comes amid continued demand growth on some routes: WorldACD recorded a 20% year-on-year increase in chargeable weight from Thailand to the US in the week to 1 November.

The Surface Transportation Board has ordered Union Pacific to turn over records concerning potential retaliation against opponents of its proposed merger with Norfolk Southern. The order follows remarks by CEO Jim Vena that customers who opposed the deal could face higher rates.
What’s Related
The board said the comments may have discouraged participation in its merger review. It warned that it “will not tolerate retaliation and will ensure that its processes are fair, transparent, and open to all stakeholders.”
Speaking at a Southwestern Association of Railroad Shippers event, Vena told attendees that Union Pacific was willing to make deals with customers. He then described what could happen if the merger did not proceed.
“If we don't do that, Union Pacific will still be there. And if I stick around, which I probably will, I'll probably increase everybody's rates that said they didn't want a seamless railroad by three or four extra percent to teach you a lesson. Thank you very much.”
Union Pacific sought to keep the remarks confidential, but the board rejected that request. It ordered the railroad to make the recording available to all parties and produce internal communications, records, and verified statements concerning potential retaliation.
RELATED: Midterm election results signal potential shifts in U.S. supply chain and freight policy
Merger opponents seek dismissal
The board also rejected Union Pacific’s request to allow private communications initiated by board members. It allowed additional parties to join the merger proceeding after the original participation deadline.
CPKC asked the board in an Oct. 30 letter to dismiss the merger application. It argued that Vena’s statements and Union Pacific’s alleged conduct had compromised the review and the board’s ability to determine whether the deal serves the public interest.
The merger applicants must respond to CPKC’s letter by Nov. 19. The board said it would address the dismissal request in a subsequent decision and consider any evidence of retaliation when deciding how the proceeding moves forward.
The Stop the Rail Merger Coalition, whose members include competing railroads, shipper organizations, and labor groups, also criticized Vena’s remarks. It argued that higher freight rates would ultimately reach consumers through higher prices for everyday goods.
Union Pacific denies retaliation
Union Pacific said it does not retaliate against customers and that their positions on the merger will not determine their rates or service. The railroad urged customers to participate in the review.
“Customers should participate freely and candidly in the Surface Transportation Board’s (STB) review,” the company said.
Union Pacific said more than 1,000 parties were participating in the proceeding, including more than 500 customers who favor the merger and account for more than 30% of its volume. It said Vena had met with hundreds of customers since the announcement.
Baird analyst Daniel Moore offered a more measured assessment in a research note issued before the board’s decision. He described Vena’s remarks as “a poor choice of words” but said they should not warrant dismissing the application.
For more details on the STB’s decision and reactions to Vena’s remarks, visit Logistics Management to read the full story.

At the American Heart Association conference, investigators were supportive of further studying Novo’s IL-6 inhibitor ziltivekimab in patients with less severe cardiovascular and kidney disease.
Novo’s IL-6 inhibitor ziltivekimab may have a future in treating less sick patients with cardiovascular and chronic kidney disease, despite a Phase 3 failure earlier this year that called the entire drug class into question.
Investigators presented follow-up results from the late-stage ZEUS trial at the American Heart Association conference in Chicago over the weekend to a standing-room-only crowd, according to BMO Capital Markets.
The study’s population ended up being heavily weighted by a high-risk group of patients with advanced cardiorenal disease who had a higher prevalence of heart failure, the investigators argued. This “raises the possibility that the mechanism was appropriate, but the population was not,” BMO wrote on Sunday.
Ziltivekimab appeared to work as intended by reducing inflammation, with an associated reduction in cholesterol. But the trial did not meet its main goal of reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events as compared to placebo.
“ZEUS reinforces that neither elevated inflammatory biomarkers nor their substantial reduction guarantees benefit across populations,” BMO wrote.

Novo’s late-stage IL-6 stumble shakes inflammation space
Novo Nordisk was banking on the inflammatory benefits of its investigational therapy ziltivekimab to improve cardiovascular outcomes. Last week’s Phase 3 failure dashed not just the Danish pharma’s hopes but that of other drugmakers working on the same pathway.

To advance ziltivekimab, Novo should focus on patient selection, the investigators said. They were generally open to further testing of the drug, supported by studies of similar therapies in the class such as Novartis’ successful Phase 3 CANTOS trial of canakinumab in 2017.
After the ZEUS failure, Novo ended several studies of ziltivekimab, including the Phase 3 HERMES and ATHENA tests. But the Phase 3 ARTEMIS trial in the acute setting is continuing on, featuring patients who have had a heart attack. The investigators noted that patients enrolled in ARTEMIS have less chronic kidney disease and heart failure as compared to ZEUS’ population, according to BMO. ZEUS’ failure sent shockwaves across the inflammatory disease space this summer, with shares tumbling for companies like BioAge Labs and Monte Rosa Therapeutics, which are developing drugs to reduce cardiovascular risk by lowering inflammation.
“The ZEUS data do not refute the broader cardiovascular inflammation hypothesis (for which there is already positive data),” BMO said.
The AHA presentation makes a case for continuing to explore inflammation reduction as a means of addressing cardiovascular disease.

By [email protected]
9 November 2026
China, India, and the Middle East are all playing their role in shifting the geographical centre of production and innovation, the three regions emerging as particularly important to the global pharmaceutical supply chain
Frank van Gelder, secretary general of Pharma.Aero, said a fracturing of the supply chain with a more geographically diffuse network of production, healthcare providers, and clinical centres could create new opportunities for airfreight and specialist logistics providers.
“China is no longer only a major source of pharmaceutical ingredients and manufacturing capacity; it is becoming an increasingly important centre for biotechnology, clinical development, and innovative medicines,” he told The Loadstar .
“India remains essential to generics and manufacturing, while expanding its innovative capabilities; Europe and North America remain central, but innovation and production are becoming more geographically distributed.
While Europe and North America would remain important pharma centres, he said the emergence of additional innovation and production hubs was creating what he called a “multi-polar pharmaceutical world”.
For logistics providers, “that means multi-node supply chains – interconnected manufacturing sites, clinical centres, specialised logistics hubs, and healthcare delivery points, rather than dependence on a few dominant origins and gateways”, Mr van Gelder explained.
“For air cargo this opens opportunities for new regional gateways and specialised corridors, but it also demands much better network orchestration,” he added. However, he cautioned that nodes must be “qualified, connected, interoperable, and economically justified”.
That meant those considering it needed to be able to distinguish between diversification and “expensive duplication”, he said, noting:“More nodes do not automatically mean greater resilience, more tonnage, or better profitability.”
And he warned that the emergence of regional gateways and specialised corridors would place greater demands on the ability of logistics operators to coordinate, given the increased complexity in these international networks.
The requirement for temperature-controlled infrastructure, qualified handling facilities, and reliable connections between different supply chain participants was particularly important as pharmaceutical products become more specialised, he added.
Mr van Gelder said: “The most profound change comes with advanced therapies. In autologous cell therapy, a patient’s cells can be collected, transported for manufacturing, and returned as a personalised treatment.
“Chain of identity, chain of custody, time, temperature, and clinical scheduling become inseparable. A disruption can affect a treatment appointment. Radioligand therapies introduce another set of highly time-sensitive, product-specific constraints,” he said.
However, Mr van Gelder cautioned against assuming the emergence of new pharmaceutical production centres or growth in innovative medicines would automatically translate into greater airfreight volumes.

By Nils Roche
9 November 2026
On the question of whether the ASX replaces the AS3, the rotations point the other way. Together they give Hapag-Lloyd two weekly sailings into the same four Brazilian gateways, each fed from a different Chinese catchment – imitating how CMA CGM and its Ocean Alliance partners pair SEAS 2 and SEAS A.
Add the slots Hapag-Lloyd buys on Maersk’s ASAS, which still calls Buenos Aires and Montevideo direct, and the Hamburg-based line covers the trade three ways.
However, we cannot exclude that ASX could serve as a policy insurance, should Hapag and Zim part ways on their joint AS3/ZFS.
Summary of recent network events (Source: Solvens Advisory)
Read the rotation, not the press release
ASX runs a port rotation of Qingdao-Ningbo-Shekou-Tanjung Pelepas-Santos-Itajaí-Rio Grande-Paranaguá-Santos-Singapore. Five choices stand out.
It gathers westbound cargo at Tanjung Pelepas, while every rival on the trade uses Singapore. The two are 30 miles apart and interchangeable for a customer’s box, so this is not about the shipper; it is about which network ASX plugs into – which matters for a different reason, outlined below.
It skips Shanghai. ASX is the only Asia–ECSA service that does not call at the largest container port on the planet. This leads towards an engineered network to work with Gemini’s shuttles.
It calls at Itajaí before Paranaguá. Most services run Santos, then Paranaguá. Hapag-Lloyd puts Santa Catarina second on discharge and pushes Paranaguá to fourth, so Paranaguá imports arrive later while its exports, loaded late in the sweep, keep a fast run to Asia.
It places Rio Grande in the middle, not at an end. Rio Grande is usually first or last, marking it as an import or an export port. Here it is the turn of the loop and the single feeder pivot for Montevideo and Buenos Aires, so it has to sit mid-string to connect the River Plate both ways.
And it reaches north to Qingdao, while not having Hong Kong on the backhaul, and imports will be left to a Singapore relay. What its presence really tells us, is that ASX & AS3 are meant to stay side by side, offering a complete portfolio of corridors to Hapag customers.
Tentative services & players in April 27 (Source: Solvens Advisory)
The tight market has an expiry date
For shippers, the timing matters more than the branding. December removes the Maersk–CMA CGM ASAS2 loop and, by my count, nominal weekly capacity from Asia falls by about 6%.
In April, MSC replaces Hapag-Lloyd’s five ships on Ipanema with its own, and Hapag-Lloyd adds a whole new loop. At ship sizes like AS3’s, that is in the order of 10,000 teu a week of extra capacity, and enough to reverse December’s cut.
Therefore, shippers signing annual contracts this winter should not price December’s tighter market as permanent.
By the second quarter next year, the Asia-east coast South America trade will be split between at least four groups that each control their own ships: the Ocean Alliance members; MSC with ONE; Maersk; and Hapag-Lloyd with or without Zim.
That is a more competitive trade than the one these partnerships created, and it arrives just as contracts signed during the squeeze start to kick in.
